analysis.one_liner: Bans any federal regulation of carbon dioxide emissions until China, India, and Russia adopt similar reductions.
analysis.headline: The bill got no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would block the EPA — and every other federal agency — from regulating carbon dioxide emissions in the United States until the Secretary of Commerce certifies in writing that China, India, and Russia have started requiring cuts substantially similar to those proposed here [S2][S3]. In effect, it makes US climate regulation hostage to three other governments' decisions. It was introduced by Senator David Vitter of Louisiana on January 25, 2011, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it remained with no further action [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be coal-fired power plants, oil refiners, and other large carbon emitters, who would have been spared the cost of emission controls and the possibility of a national carbon cap indefinitely, since the bill's own condition depends on actions by foreign governments that the record does not suggest were imminent. Electric utilities and fossil fuel producers would keep their current cost structure regardless of carbon pollution.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the EPA Administrator and every other federal agency head from regulating carbon dioxide emissions until Commerce certifies that China, India, and Russia have initiated substantially similar required reductions [S2][S3].
Uses language that overrides any other provision of law ('notwithstanding any other provision of law'), so the ban would apply even where existing statutes authorize carbon regulation [S3].

Places the trigger entirely in the hands of the Secretary of Commerce's written certification, meaning no US carbon rules could take effect until an executive branch official verified comparable foreign action [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on ordinary people in the form of continued unregulated carbon dioxide emissions — with the health and climate consequences that follow — while governments and businesses elsewhere face no comparable constraint on their emissions, since the US rulemaking power would be suspended until three foreign governments act.

drawbacks.text: The bill would indefinitely delay US carbon regulation, because it conditions any rule on emissions reductions from China, India, and Russia that are 'substantially similar' to what is proposed for the United States — a standard requiring certification by the Secretary of Commerce with no deadline or fallback [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection a supporter would raise in its favor — that the US acting alone imposes costs on domestic energy producers while other large emitters keep emitting — is itself the bill's premise, and the bill offers no mechanism to actually secure foreign reductions, only a prohibition until they appear [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades short-term cost relief for large emitters against an indefinite delay in addressing carbon emissions. Its condition — verified 'substantially similar' reductions in three foreign countries — gives US emitters a permanent pass if those countries never meet it, and even supporters of coordinating climate policy internationally would concede the bill pursues that goal purely by prohibiting domestic action rather than by negotiating anything. The costs land broadly on the public; the benefits are concentrated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter (R-LA) introduced S. 15 on January 25, 2011, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S5].
No cosponsors signed on; the cosponsor list shows zero [S4].
The action history shows no further steps after the committee referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people are arguably better off that the bill died, since it would have frozen US carbon regulation until conditions in three foreign governments' policies were certified. The bill's potential beneficiaries — large carbon emitters — gained nothing concrete either, because the regulation it sought to block was already facing other obstacles and the bill never advanced. The clearest 'winner' is the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; the bill went nowhere

for.name: Sen. David Vitter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee, where it sat with no further action; no senators signed on as cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew zero cosponsors from either party and never reached a vote, so the record contains no vote breakdown and no organized opposition inside the chamber — it simply attracted no visible support [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and gas producers and large carbon emitters (power plants, refineries)
industries.note: The bill would have removed the threat of federal carbon regulation indefinitely by conditioning it on certified reductions in China, India, and Russia. The industry's gain is the public's continued exposure to unregulated carbon emissions.
